summary: Cleveland NF tower on Hot Springs Mountain, San Diego County's highest point; current 1942 cab partly fallen, unstaffed, on Los Coyotes land with climbing prohibited.

facts.design: Region 5 design C-3 wood 14 x 14 ft cab on a new 20 ft tower (1942); earlier 4AR 14 x 14 cab on a 23 ft timber tower (1928)
facts.status_note: still standing but badly decayed: pieces of the cab have fallen to the ground and the roof has collapsed (NHLR 2017 visit report; FFLA); FFLA says the last set of pictures shows the structure about to fall

staffing.status: unstaffed; the 2017 visit report lists no volunteer openings

access.note: on Los Coyotes Reservation land; the tribe allows hiking from its campgrounds on a purchased or prepaid permit; the approach road has a chain gate opened with a key from the visitors' booth; the reservation recently reopened to public visitation

visit.trail_note: high-clearance vehicle needed on the roughly 5-mile approach road (2017 visit report); the tribe says the tower is not the summit and climbing is prohibited

events.note: first lookout, a 7 x 7 ft ground house constructed by the Cleveland National Forest
June 1913 newspaper describes a one-room frame building on the summit boulder, with a map table used to plot smoke bearings
second structure, a 4AR 14 x 14 ft cab on a 23 ft timber tower, replaced the original
June 1937: a crew of carpenters and material were packed in to the lookout, which a column says cannot be reached by automobile; the excerpt does not name the work
August 1939: lookout William Charlton fled when flames threatened the tower
present cab and tower built: Register Built field 1942; upgraded with a Region 5 design C-3 cab and new 20 ft tower
June 21, 2017 NHLR visit report: advanced state of decay, pieces of the cab fallen on the west side, stairs dangerous, unstaffed

corrections.current: The tower still stands, but its cab is gone (FFLA).
corrections.proposed: The tower still stands, but parts of the cab have fallen and the roof has collapsed.
corrections.why: FFLA says the roof has collapsed and the glass and furnishings are gone; it does not say the cab is gone. The NHLR June 2017 visit report says pieces of the cab structure have fallen to the ground.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give 1912, 1928 and 1942. The 1912 and 1928 dates describe earlier structures, and the 1942 date describes the present cab and tower. The NHLR Built field and the 1942 upgrade describe the same structure, so the brief's separate '1942 built' and '1942 replaced' entries are one event.

The Register calls the first lookout a 7 x 7 ft ground house built in 1912. A June 1913 newspaper describes a one-room frame building on the summit boulder. The story reports both and does not say they are the same building.

notes_for_editor: Condition rests on the NHLR June 2017 visit report, the undated FFLA page and a directory's 'Collapsing' entry; no newer visit was found. The 1928 and 1942 structures are described consistently by NHLR and FFLA. The 1913 Daybook frame building is not reconciled with the Register's 1912 ground house. The brief's 'cab is gone' is corrected. The directory row for Hot Springs reads Collapsing; 'Red-tagged - structural' on the same page belongs to High Point. Elevation: NHLR 6,535 ft; FFLA 6,533 ft. Access is permission-only in practice; no climbing invitation is made. Checked 2026-10-08: the 2017 approach-road wording is now 'says ... is required' (the Register says 'required'), not 'advises'. The tower-stands wording now cites both the Register and FFLA ('about to fall'). William Charlton is named in the August 14, 1939 excerpt quoted from The San Bernardino County Sun.
